idiom_name: overloaded functions on concrete types for closed sets; protocols (witness tables) for generic customization
implementation_notes: Swift resolves overloads statically from the types at the call site, and the compiler's own diagnostics recommend exactly this for static dispatch: use function overloading to provide a separate function with the same name for every concrete type, because knowing the exact type at compile time enables inlining and the rest of the optimizer. So for a closed set of types, an overload set on concrete or marker types is a genuine realization and the closure is checked by the compiler. Inside generic code, however, the customization point is a protocol requirement dispatched through a witness table, and specialization/devirtualization are SIL optimizer passes rather than language semantics: the compiler team states that selection among ad-hoc overloads is performed statically from local knowledge and stays consistent across all specializations of a generic function, which is precisely why a C++-style trait-mapped ladder cannot be reproduced. What replaces the classic structure: overloads for concrete types, protocol requirements plus generic constraints for code that must stay generic. The classic form is justified exactly when the type is known at the call site or the case set is closed; otherwise use a protocol.
pitfalls: @_specialize is an underscored attribute and merely a hint: it does not change which implementation a generic call resolves to, it only asks the optimizer to emit a specialized copy, so it cannot be used to select behaviour.

Methods declared in a protocol extension but not in the protocol requirement list are dispatched statically to the extension's implementation even for conforming types, so a 'tag path' added in an extension can be bypassed without a diagnostic.

Reaching for an existential (any Protocol) to make the ladder generic always dispatches through the witness table, silently reinstating the runtime cost - and overloads on existential versus concrete types can create ambiguity that the compiler reports at the call site.

Value types passed through generic code get static dispatch only after specialization; whether that happens depends on whole-module optimization and access (for example @inlinable), so identical source can perform differently across modules.

Knowing the exact object type at compile time enables the whole suite of compiler optimizations.', https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/d06e05fc6d0f6827066e05d5c2ac40a6f23852d1/userdocs/diagnostics/existential-type.md
